newsitem.title: HONG KONG: YEAREND - Asia '97 gold view upbeat, worries remain.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Asia '97 gold view upbeat, worries remain.

text.p: Asian gold dealers are fairly upbeat about the precious metal's prospects next year despite the price retreats of recent months, although nagging worries remain over institutional and producer sales spilling into 1997.
Dealers across Asia said they expect gold demand to hold up, although Taiwan's trade struck a more gloomy note.
"I still think Asia will be a major consumer and consumption will be growing at 10 percent in 1997," said Raymond Chan Fat-chu, president of Hong Kong's Chinese Gold and Silver Exchange Society.

Chan also forecast that gold demand in the colony could jump by as much as 20 percent next year, boosted by tourist purchases as visitors flock to Hong Kong to experience the British handover to China on June 30.
In India, the world's biggest gold market, analysts forecast lower prices in 1997 and said this could boost the country's gold imports beyond the current 500 tonnes a year.

Gold demand in China, the world's fourth largest consumer, could surge as much as 10 percent in 1997 to 246 tonnes, with the biggest demand increase coming from secondary cities, the World Gold Council's Hong Kong and South China manager Emily Li said in an interview earlier this month.

South Korea's largest gold producer, LG Metals Corp, said the nation's gold consumption in wedding and jewellery gifts would remain steady next year, as would demand from the semiconductor industry despite the sector's losses this year.
The country's actual gold consumption was expected to rise slightly to 100 tonnes next year from an estimated 95 tonnes in 1996, said Lee Gook-ho, an executive director at LG Metals.
Oh Tae-hwan, a general manager at South Korea's leading bullion house Daewoo Corp, said he expected the company's gold trade to remain steady next year at around the 1996 level of 150 tonnes.
Taiwan's gold market, however, is forecast to remain sluggish after imports hit a monthly peak of 25.24 tonnes during military friction with China in March 1this year, traders said.

A renewed flareup in tensions between Taiwan and China could spark a gold rush, but that prospect looks increasingly remote given the warming ties between Beijing and Washington, a Taiwanese dealer said.
PRODUCER AND CENTRAL BANK GOLD SELLING WORRIES REMAIN

Anxiety in Asia over central bank and producer gold sales will continue to throw a pall over bullish sentiment in 1997. "Possible gold sales by European central banks and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), combined with expected producer selling on any price rebound, will continue to cast a shadow on the market," said Jun Ohtaguro, a dealer at Tokyo's Nissho Iwai Corp.
Gains in gold prices could be countered by miners' sales.
"Any move toward $390 per ounce or above would see strong producer forward selling, thus bringing the price back down," said Paul Gooday, an analyst in Sydney at AME Mineral Economics.
He added that huge stockpiles of gold held by financial institutions were the most significant factor overhanging the market.

Gold prices were likely to be subdued further by increasing mine supplies, growing at 5.6 percent a year compared with gold fabrication demand increasing at only 3.27 percent, said Simon Middleton an analyst at the official Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics in Canberra.
GOLD PRICE FORECASTS FOR 1997 VARY CONSIDERABLY
Price expectations for gold in 1997 vary widely in the region with the South Koreans and Australians offering the most bullish forecasts ranging between $381-$395 an ounce.
South Korea's LG Metals Corp said it forecast an average spot gold price next year of between $385 to $395 an ounce. It saw the lowest price at $375 and the highest at $410.
These forecasts were followed closely by the Japanese and the Taiwanese who between them estimated prices within a slightly lower range of between $370-$380 an ounce.

"Gold is likely to benefit from funds' money shifting to the gold market from the U.S. stock market as the U.S. stocks are now overvalued and set for corrections," said Makoto Tonoki, general manager of Tanaka Kikinzoku Kogyo K.K.'s precious metals division
The Singaporean and Hong Kong dealers polled proved most pessimistic, forecasting a price range between $340-$370 an ounce in 1997.

"Interest rates will remain at a low level, so that stock markets and bond markets will remain strong," said Jason Wong, senior manager at Hong Kong-based Po Sang Bank Ltd, adding that the US dollar would also stay firm and gold prices in terms of yen or European currencies will not be cheap.
